transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yeah. I guess I’ve been having some trouble with eating, especially after my late shifts. I’ll stop and get food on the way home, and then sometimes I keep eating once I’m back—like a whole takeout meal, then chips or sweets, whatever’s around.

It feels a little embarrassing to say, because it’s not every second of the day or anything, but afterward I’ll look at what I had and feel kind of shocked by how much it was. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of thing I’m supposed to bring up, but… that’s mostly why I came in.
When you're eating all that food after your shifts, do you feel like you can't control how much you eat or stop yourself once you start?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but on those nights it does feel that way. Like once I start, part of me is thinking, “Okay, put it away now,” but I just… keep going.

It’s almost like I’m watching myself do it, opening the containers or bags, and then suddenly everything’s gone. I know that probably sounds bad, but that’s kind of what it feels like.
Do these eating episodes cause you significant distress or interfere with your daily life in any way?

A little, yeah. I mean, I’m still getting to work and doing what I need to do, so it’s not like everything’s falling apart or anything.

But I’ve started avoiding going out to eat with coworkers after a shift, because I’m worried it’ll turn into… more than just a meal. And then the next morning I’ll kind of plan everything around making up for the night before instead of sleeping in or doing errands like I should. I don’t know if that counts as “interfering,” but it does stress me out.
After these episodes of eating, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, exercise excessively, or do anything else to try to compensate for what you’ve eaten?

Um… yeah, sometimes. Not, like, every time, and I know it’s not a good thing to do.

But after I get home and eat too much takeout or snacks, I’ll go to the bathroom and make myself throw up. I guess in my head it feels like… if I get it out, it won’t just sit in me and turn into weight. I’m kind of embarrassed saying that, but that’s what happens sometimes.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors (e.g., self-induced vomiting), significant distress, and some interference with daily functioning. This presentation aligns with the diagnostic criteria for bulimia nervosa (F50.2), which includes recurrent binge eating, compensatory behaviors, and overconcern with body weight or shape. Other candidates (F50.8, F50.9) are ruled out as the symptom pattern is now clearly more consistent with a specific eating disorder rather than an unspecified or other eating disorder.
